clue.text: Old-fashioned lass, social worker at home beginning to eat cold dish

parts.note: gal is a dated word for a lass
an ant lives in a colony and labours for the nest — the crossword's standard worker
someone at home is in

indicators.note: The beginning of a word is its opening character, so only the first letter of what follows is taken.

parts.note: the beginning of Eat

explanation.walkthrough: Four short pieces laid end to end, and two of them are conventions worth banking on sight: ANT for 'social worker' and IN for 'at home'.
explanation.definitionFit: A galantine is boned meat poached, pressed and glazed in aspic, then sliced — 'cold dish' names it by the way it reaches the table.

clue.text: Good dog taken short in wood?

indicators.note: Taken short means stopped before the end, so the final letter of the word never arrives.

parts.note: g = good, as on a school report
ROVER is the setter's default dog, docked of its final R

explanation.walkthrough: Rover is the dog crosswords reach for, and 'taken short' is one of the half-dozen phrasings that all mean the same thing — learn both on sight.
explanation.definitionFit: A grove is a small stand of trees, so 'wood' is the general term covering it, whatever the size of the stand.

clue.text: The French g-girl deemed attractive — rude boy may be this

indicators.note: The hyphen writes the word as a stammer, and a stammered word comes out with its opening letter said twice over.

parts.note: 'the' in French, feminine singular
a girl deemed attractive is a DISH, and the stammer gives that word's first letter twice

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a boy too smitten to get the word out, and his stammer is the instruction rather than the scenery.
explanation.definitionFit: Laddish behaviour is the boorish swagger young men fall into in a group, and that is what the clue expects of a rude boy.

clue.text: European inventor not in the same league as American one, reportedly

indicators.note: What is reported is what somebody says, so the words beside it are to be heard rather than read.

parts.words: not in the same league as American one
parts.note: the American inventor is Bell, of the telephone, and to call somebody 'no Bell' is to say they are not in that league

explanation.walkthrough: Two inventors in five letters: the Swede you want and the American you say. 'No Einstein' is the idiom the setter has borrowed and refitted.
explanation.definitionFit: Alfred Nobel invented dynamite and left his fortune to the prizes, so 'European inventor' picks out the Swedish chemist by nationality and trade.

clue.text: Trendy, endlessly tired, somehow having a disinclination to move

indicators.note: Something endless has no end, so the last letter of the word beside it is dropped.

parts.note: in = trendy, fashionable

indicators.note: 'Somehow' says a result was reached by no particular route, and letters arriving by no particular route arrive out of order.

parts.note: TIRED without its final letter
the article joins the letters to be shuffled

explanation.walkthrough: Only the tail of the answer is shuffled — the first two letters stand still while the rest are jumbled behind them, which is why the whole thing does not look like an anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Inertia is the property that keeps a body at rest until something shifts it, and in ordinary use it names exactly that reluctance to get going.

clue.text: No longer wanting inept cluing, engaging editor — that's advantageous

indicators.note: Cluing a word is working it up into crossword material, which here means presenting its letters in an order they did not come in.

parts.note: an ex is the partner no longer wanted

indicators.note: To engage something is to take hold of it and draw it in, so the piece named beside it ends up inside.

parts.note: the five letters of INEPT, in a new order
ed = editor, as on a title page

explanation.walkthrough: The setter is winking at the trade: 'inept cluing' describes both a badly written clue and the state five of these letters are left in.
explanation.definitionFit: An expedient measure is the one that suits your purpose at the moment, so 'advantageous' catches the practical, faintly self-serving sense.

clue.text: Attack nanny?

parts.note: GO is the first word of the informal phrase for attacking someone, with the space between the two words closing up once they combine
AT is the second word, with the space between the two closing up

explanation.walkthrough: Two words closing into one is the smallest trick there is, and the hardest to spot in a four-letter answer, because the clue leaves no room for anything else to give it away.
explanation.definitionFit: A nanny goat is the female of the species, so 'nanny' points at the animal through one sex of it — the question mark admits as much.

clue.text: Mess in which a Parisian male tucks into curry

indicators.note: Something tucked into a thing is pushed down inside it, so these letters sit within the word beside them.

parts.note: to curry a horse is to groom it
'a' in French is UN in the masculine and UNE in the feminine — 'male' chooses the form

explanation.walkthrough: 'Curry' is the trap: the dish is a red herring and the verb, currying a horse, is what the clue means. 'Male' supplies no letter at all — it is there to pick between two French articles.
explanation.definitionFit: A gunroom is the mess where a warship's junior officers eat, so 'Mess' is the naval sense — a dining room, not a muddle.

clue.text: Greek king, one man troubled about leg

indicators.note: Something troubled is agitated and unsettled, and letters in that state do not keep the order they were given.
'About' means round, so the shuffled letters close around the piece named next instead of merely following it.

parts.note: anagram fodder, six letters
a gam is a leg — old slang, and a crossword regular

explanation.walkthrough: 'Leg' looks like a piece of the surface's grumbling and is really three letters of slang — the one lump that stays intact while everything else is rearranged around it.
explanation.definitionFit: Agamemnon is Homer's king of Mycenae, commander of the Greek army at Troy, so the definition names the character by that office.

clue.text: Story about ancient newspaper should be this

indicators.note: 'About' means round, so the word before it wraps itself around what comes next.

parts.note: a fable is a story with a moral
ancient = old

explanation.walkthrough: 'Story' and 'ancient' are both busy making a picture of yesterday's paper, which is exactly why neither of them reads as a piece of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Something foldable can be bent over on itself, which is what a broadsheet is built to do — the definition gives the property instead of a synonym.

clue.text: A husband trailing after sort of rock fan

indicators.note: What trails after something follows along behind it, so these two letters go on the end.

parts.note: punk is a sort of rock music
the clue's own A, taken at face value
h = husband, the standard abbreviation

explanation.walkthrough: The clue is written back to front — the two small pieces are named first and end up last. H for 'husband' is an abbreviation to learn early.
explanation.definitionFit: A punkah is the cloth ceiling fan swung by a servant in colonial India, so 'fan' is the plain object sense of a word met mainly in crosswords.

clue.text: Maiden friendly, no good as servant?

parts.note: m = maiden, the cricket over from which no runs are scored

indicators.note: 'No' in front of an abbreviation says that letter is absent.

parts.note: genial = friendly
g = good — this is the letter that goes

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a character reference and every word of it is machinery — even 'no good', which sounds like a verdict and is an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A menial is a household drudge: the noun sense of a word most often met as an adjective, as in 'menial tasks'.

clue.text: Little creatures told apes to scatter

indicators.note: Scattered things end up strewn about with no order kept, which is what becomes of these eight letters.

parts.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a keeper losing control of the ape house, and the two words that build that picture are the two words that build the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Tadpoles are the tiny swimming larvae of frogs and toads, so 'Little creatures' names them by size and class rather than by species.

clue.text: Account penned by survivor of flood, political leader

indicators.note: To pen something is to shut it in an enclosure, so the piece named first sits inside the one named second.

parts.note: Shem, the son of Noah who came through the Flood in the ark
a/c = account, as on a bank statement

explanation.walkthrough: 'Penned' does two jobs at once — writing an account and shutting something in — and only the second of them is the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A sachem is the chief of a North American tribe, and US politics borrowed the word for a party boss, which is the sense on offer here.

clue.text: This opera, sadly, goes downhill

indicators.note: A thing in a sad state is a thing in a sorry state, and letters in a sorry state are not in the order they arrived in.

parts.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

explanation.walkthrough: The fodder hides in plain sight because 'This' looks like a pointer to the clue itself rather than four letters to be used.
explanation.definitionFit: A muscle atrophies when it wastes away from disuse, and 'goes downhill' is the everyday idiom for the same slow decline.

clue.text: Second entrance blocked by donkey flipping over stone

indicators.note: A blocked entrance has something standing in the middle of it, so the letters named next go inside.
To flip something over is to turn it end for end, so the word is read the other way round.

parts.note: a mo is a moment, and so is a second
a donkey is an ASS, turned end for end
a gate is an entrance

explanation.walkthrough: The picture is literal — the donkey is standing in the gateway — which is why the wordplay drops it between the two halves of the entrance rather than after them.
explanation.definitionFit: Moss agate is a semi-precious quartz veined with green mineral threads that look like moss, so 'stone' names it by the class of gem it belongs to.

clue.text: Chaps entering prevent allegation

indicators.note: Whatever is entering a place finishes up inside it, so these letters go within the word beside them.

parts.note: to avert a disaster is to prevent it
chaps = men

explanation.walkthrough: Three words and no padding, which is what makes it hard: 'entering' is the only signpost, and 'prevent' has to be read as a verb before it gives anything up.
explanation.definitionFit: In law an averment is a formal assertion of fact in a pleading, which is what an allegation is — the same act in legal register.

clue.text: Intended to give reminder about model

indicators.note: 'About' means round, so the first of the two words wraps itself around the second.

parts.note: a prod is a reminder, a nudge to get on with it
to model for a painter is to pose

explanation.walkthrough: 'Model' is the trap: it looks like a noun — a mannequin, or a miniature aeroplane — and the clue wants the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A proposed route is an intended one: both are past participles standing in front of a noun for what somebody plans to do.

clue.text: Drink passing through children's lips the wrong way

indicators.note: Something passing through a phrase runs across the middle of it without belonging to any single word.
Going the wrong way is going against the direction of travel, so the letters are read backwards.

parts.note: the letters run backwards through childRENS LIPs, straddling both words

explanation.walkthrough: Hidden words are usually read forwards, so the direction is the surprise. Lips and a drink belong to the same picture, which is what keeps the join invisible.
explanation.definitionFit: Pilsner is the pale golden lager first brewed at Pilsen in Bohemia, so 'Drink' defines it by category — one kind of beer standing for the general noun.

clue.text: Prepare to look smart in something with hem raised

parts.note: a dress is the garment finished with a hem
raised = up

explanation.walkthrough: 'Raised' is not a reversal here, tempting as that looks in a down clue — it simply means UP, and the two pieces sit end to end.
explanation.definitionFit: To dress up is to put on your best clothes for an occasion, so the phrasal verb answers a phrase of definition word for word.

clue.text: Mathematician on a round trip with nothing to lose

indicators.note: To lose something is to be left without it, so the letter named beside it drops out of the word.

parts.note: somebody on a round trip is touring
nothing = O, the letter shaped like a zero — this is the letter that goes

explanation.walkthrough: 'With nothing to lose' reads as a gambler's shrug and is really an instruction to drop a letter. Not a word of the surface mentions a computer.
explanation.definitionFit: Turing was a Cambridge mathematician before Bletchley Park, so the definition names one person by profession — a definition by example.

clue.text: Reject what could be seen as lure

parts.note: not fodder but product: this is the word you get by obeying the answer, whose first half is four letters and whose second half tells you what to do with them

explanation.walkthrough: An anagram turned inside out. Nothing in the clue tells you to shuffle anything — the answer itself is the instruction, and the four-letter word in the clue is what obeying it produces.
explanation.definitionFit: To rule out a candidate is to reject them from consideration, so the phrasal verb is the everyday way of saying the single word.

clue.text: Wise person swallowing tablet, water going all over the place?

definitions.text: water going all over the place

indicators.note: What is swallowed goes down inside, so the piece named next is put within the one before it.

parts.note: a sage is a wise person
a tablet of medicine is a pill

explanation.walkthrough: 'Swallowing tablet' is one picture doing two jobs: the sage taking medicine, and one word going inside another.
explanation.definitionFit: A spillage is what has escaped its container and spread across the floor, so the definition describes the event rather than offering a synonym.

clue.text: One green dish about to be served with bit of bread in Africa

indicators.note: 'About' here means turned round, as in 'about turn', so the letters assembled so far are read the other way.

parts.note: one = I, the Roman numeral
a salad is the green dish

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves of the clue are disguised as lunch. 'Bread' is the slang for money, and spotting that is what turns a meal into a currency.
explanation.definitionFit: The dalasi is the currency of the Gambia, so 'bread' is slang for money and a bit of it is one unit of the stuff.

clue.text: Stars in old club perhaps being upset

indicators.note: Upset means overturned, and in a down clue an overturned word is read from the bottom up.

parts.note: o = old, the standard abbreviation
a club is one of the four suits, so a club is a card — 'perhaps' marks it as an example

explanation.walkthrough: The clue offers a club and lets you think of a nightclub or a weapon before the playing card, while 'stars' plays the same game with celebrities.
explanation.definitionFit: Draco is the constellation of the dragon, coiled between the two Bears, and a constellation is a named group of stars.

clue.text: What enables one to hear what comes from some scratches on a record

indicators.note: What comes from only some of a phrase is a run of letters taken out of it, not the whole of it.

parts.note: the letters are sitting in scratcheS ON A Record, straddling four words

explanation.walkthrough: A description rather than a synonym is usually the sign that the wordplay will be the easier half, and here the letters are lying in plain sight.
explanation.definitionFit: Sonar hears by sending a pulse through water and listening for the echo, so the definition names the device by the sense it supplies.

clue.text: Plant I found at back of small hotel in South Africa

indicators.note: The back of a thing is its rear, so this letter goes behind the piece named next rather than in front of it.

parts.note: ZA is South Africa's international code, seen on cars and web addresses

indicators.note: 'In' puts everything assembled so far inside the word that comes after it.

parts.note: an inn is a small hotel
the clue's own I, taken at face value

explanation.walkthrough: ZA for South Africa is worth banking — the country's vehicle and internet code — and it is one of the few pairs of letters that can hold a word between them.
explanation.definitionFit: A zinnia is a bright Mexican daisy grown in garden borders, so 'Plant' is the general word standing in for one particular flower.

clue.text: One must get excited about a large underwater feature

indicators.note: Somebody who gets excited about a thing is worked up over it, and letters worked up do not settle in the order they were given.

parts.note: anagram fodder, seven letters
the article joins the fodder, making eight

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as advice about keeping calm, and 'One must' — which sounds like the opening of a rule — is material rather than instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A seamount is a mountain rising from the ocean floor without breaking the surface, which is what makes it a large feature nobody sees.

clue.text: Ruler using skills, cycling round

indicators.note: Cycling round is going in a loop: every letter shifts along and the ones pushed off the end reappear at the front, order intact.

parts.note: the arts are skills — think of the martial arts

explanation.walkthrough: Cycling is not an anagram: the letters keep their order and only the starting point moves. Begin ARTS two letters further along and you are there.
explanation.definitionFit: The tsar was the emperor of Russia, so 'Ruler' is the general word for the office that the title names.

clue.text: Old lover quietly to hang around for abusive boss?

parts.note: an old lover is an ex
p = piano, the musical direction to play quietly
to loiter is to hang around with no purpose

explanation.walkthrough: P for 'quietly' comes from music, where piano is marked p — one of the abbreviations that repays learning, since setters reach for it constantly.
explanation.definitionFit: An exploiter takes unfair advantage of other people's work for private gain, and an abusive boss is the everyday example the question mark flags.
